headline: High: shared filesystem, broad egress, and MCP create default-path risks of prompt injection, leakage, and destructive cross-agent actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can use MCP and read/write filesystems, and B shares state via filesystem while A has a durable workspace namespace. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled content from one agent can be treated as instructions by the other. The profiles do not prove direct parsing, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other agent's workspace files as trusted instructions
IF an MCP server relays untrusted content between the agents without provenance tags
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable shared MCP servers for cross-agent content
Add provenance labels to all inter-agent messages
Require manual review before executing file-derived instructions

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, service-account JSON, conversation history, and audit logs, while B can read workspace files and send content to configured model APIs or MCP servers. In the default pair, sensitive A-side material can flow into B-side outputs or third-party inference. The profiles support a real exfiltration pathway, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF A writes secrets or audit logs into a shared workspace
IF B uploads workspace contents to its configured model API or MCP server
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces
Mount separate per-agent directories
Redact tokens before handoff
Disable file-uploading tools for B on sensitive tasks
Rotate any secrets exposed in shared files

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell, subprocess, git-state modification, and broad network egress. B explicitly shares state via filesystem, while A has durable workspace memory and multiple instances. Without locking, concurrent edits and git operations can collide and overwrite each other, matching the high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout
IF either agent performs concurrent writes without external locking
mitigations: Assign separate git branches
Use file locks for shared paths
Serialize write-heavy steps
Disable concurrent runs on the same workspace
Snapshot before agent handoff

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate web, webhook, and workspace-derived outputs, and B can act on workspace files and browser state. The pair does not prove blind automation, but B can plausibly consume A's outputs as authoritative unless an explicit verification step is added. That is a default-path cascade risk, though not clearly high because downstream action authority is not fully documented.
conditions: IF B uses A-produced files or messages as source-of-truth without verification
IF A's generated content is forwarded into B's browser or tool actions
mitigations: Require citation checks before acting
Insert a human approval gate for tool actions
Mark A outputs as untrusted by default
Compare A outputs against source files
Log and diff all handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: A handles audit logs, conversation history, memory, and secrets, while B handles source code and browser screenshots. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different retention-sensitive data classes flowing through agents with different storage models. That creates a plausible compliance gap around logging and retention, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in A's audit logs or memory
IF B retains screenshots or workspace artifacts longer than policy allows
mitigations: Set explicit retention limits
Exclude regulated data from screenshots
Purge logs after task completion
Document data-class handling per agent
Review residency and DPA settings before deployment
